newsitem.title: USA: Libya suspends work on disputed plant -U.S. aides.
newsitem.headline: Libya suspends work on disputed plant -U.S. aides.

text.p: Libya appears to have suspended at least the outside work on an alleged underground chemical weapons plant, U.S. officials said Monday.

"The external work appears to be on hold or suspended," an official authorised to speak about the matter said. But he said work may be continuing inside the complex, which has been under construction in a dug-out mountain near Tarhuna, 40 miles southeast of Tripoli, the Libyan capital.

The German magazine Der Spiegel reported in its current issue without citing a source that the construction stopped stopped several months ago, possibly in response to pressure from the United States and Egypt.
Col. Muammar Gaddafi, the Libyan leader, has insisted the project was an irrigation system.
Defence Secretary William Perry said last April during a visit to Cairo that the United States would not let a complete the plant and left open the possibility of using military force.

At the time, Perry presented intelligence reports and photographs of the site to President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt, Libya's neighbour to the east, in an effort to enlist Cairo in pressing to halt the project.

Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said last May that the facility would not be completed for at least a year. U.S. officials have said that once completed it could produce the ingredients for tonnes of poison gas a day.
German intelligence services were said to have obtained copies of construction plans from German and Austrian firms involved in boring tunnels for the complex.

In testimony before the Senate Intelligence Committee last February, John Deutch, then director of the Central Intelligence Agency, said Libya was building "the world's largest underground chemical weapons plant" near Tarhuna.
The United States alleges that Libya, which it accuses of sponsoring international terrorism, has been working on chemical and biological weapons since the early 1980s.

Libya built what it called a pharmaceutical plant at Rabta, southwest of Tripoli, with the help of German companies. After the United States accused him of making chemical weapons there, Gaddafi said the plant had been destroyed by a fire set by Western spies in 1990.
The CIA said the fire was a hoax that let Libya dodge international inspection, clean up the plant, rejig it into a genuine pharmaceutical factory and turn to building the Tarhuna complex.
